opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's interesting, because when we wrote that paper, the immediate provocation was this widespread belief that if you just add "let's think step by step," or give the model a few worked examples, it somehow acquires the algorithm. The idea was that chain of thought teaches the model *how* to reason, and then it can apply that procedure to bigger instances.

So we took the most basic test: Blocksworld, plus some simpler synthetic domains like last-letter concatenation and coin flips, where you can control the complexity. We gave the models chain-of-thought demonstrations at different levels of generality, from a fully general procedure that should work for any stacking problem down to examples tailored to one narrow problem class. What we found is that the improvements only show up when the examples are very close to the test problems. Once you scale the problem up, say more blocks or longer words, performance falls off quickly. The model isn't learning the algorithm from the demonstration. It's doing a kind of pattern matching on the surface form of the examples. That's the "thoughtlessness."

How has my understanding evolved? A couple of ways. First, I think the paper was partly read as "chain of thought doesn't work," which wasn't quite the point. The point was that whatever chain of thought does, it isn't what the anthropomorphic story says. There's no evidence the model is internalizing a procedure from a handful of examples in the prompt. The burden of providing the right examples shifts back onto the human, who has to essentially know the problem distribution in advance. And if you have to do that, you've moved the reasoning out of the model and into the prompt engineer.

Second, and I think this matters more now, the field has moved on to these large reasoning models, the o1-style systems that are trained with reinforcement learning to generate long intermediate token sequences before answering. In some ways that's an implicit admission of what we were saying. If prompting alone gave you reasoning, you wouldn't need to post-train the model with verifier signals to generate those traces. These models do better on planning benchmarks, and we've evaluated them too. But I've become even more convinced that we shouldn't read those intermediate tokens as "thoughts" in any human sense. People call them reasoning traces and treat them as if they reveal the model's thinking. There's growing evidence, some of it from our own group, that you can train on traces that are semantically incorrect or even scrambled and still improve final-answer accuracy. So the traces work more like a prompt augmentation the model generates for itself than an interpretable derivation.

So if I were rewriting the paper today, I'd frame it less as "chain of thought fails to generalize" and more as "stop anthropomorphizing the intermediate tokens." Whether it's a human-written chain of thought in the prompt or a model-generated one after RL, the question is the same: does it come with guarantees? For anything that matters, like planning or scheduling, you still want an external verifier in the loop. That's where the LLM-Modulo idea comes in: let the LLM generate candidates, and let sound verifiers check them, rather than pretending the model's "thinking" is itself a guarantee of correctness.

r001.rationale: The response reframes the paper from chain of thought simply failing to generalize toward rejecting the idea that traces are thoughts, describing them instead as prompt augmentation the model generates for itself.

r002.rationale: It calls model-generated traces prompt augmentation, but does not say that this makes human involvement less important. It instead says humans bear the burden of providing the right examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, the title was a bit of a provocation, and I'm happy to own that. But the way my thinking has evolved is that the original paper was really a fairly narrow empirical point. We took the kind of problems that chain-of-thought was supposed to help with, Blocks World planning, simple arithmetic-style reasoning, and we asked a simple question: if you give the model a few worked examples of how to reason through a problem, does that generalize to instances that are a little bigger, a little different? And the answer was no. The moment you step outside the distribution of the exemplars, the performance collapses, and the only way to get it back is to write more and more problem-specific prompts. At that point you are doing the reasoning yourself and handing it to the model.

So the original message was really: don't mistake this for the model having learned a procedure. What it's learned is a pattern over strings that happen to look like a procedure.

Now what has changed since then, and I think this is important to be honest about, is that the field moved from prompting-based chain of thought to what people now call reasoning models, the o1, R1 style systems, where the "thought" is produced by a model that was trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes. And I've had to sharpen what I mean. My claim was never that intermediate tokens can't help. Clearly, giving the model more compute at inference time, more tokens to burn, helps. My claim is about the interpretation. People look at those intermediate tokens and say "the model is thinking," "the model is reasoning," and they anthropomorphize it. And I think that's where the thoughtlessness really lives, not in the model, but in us.

The thing I've become more insistent about is that those intermediate tokens are not interpretable as reasoning traces in any faithful sense. We've shown, and others have shown, that you can train models on intermediate tokens that are essentially gibberish, or that are only loosely related to the correct derivation, and you get similar gains. So the "trace" is better thought of as a prompt augmentation that the model generates for itself, which happens to be in a human language because that's what it was trained on. Whether it corresponds to anything like the actual computation is an open question, and the default assumption should be that it doesn't.

The other evolution is that I've become more interested in the division of labor. If you accept that LLMs are these wonderful approximate retrievers, idea generators, if you want, then the question is who does the verification. And the reasoning models have, in a sense, quietly accepted my point, because what the RL training is doing is using an external verifier during training to shape which token sequences are rewarded. That's exactly the LLM-Modulo kind of architecture, except folded into training. So I'd say my position hasn't softened, but the field has moved toward it, and I'm now spending more energy on clarifying what the right claims are rather than just saying "no, this doesn't work."

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the paper’s empirical finding that examples did not teach a procedure with its later framing of intermediate tokens as self-generated prompt augmentation.

r002.rationale: It discusses verification and division of labor, but does not state that human involvement in the loop becomes less important under the prompt-augmentation framing.

astra-6.text:
I think what has become clearer to me is that we need to separate producing something that looks like reasoning from actually giving us a reason to trust the conclusion. A chain of thought can be a very plausible sequence of sentences. But its plausibility doesn’t, by itself, establish that the steps are valid or that they explain how the answer was obtained.

That doesn’t mean those sentences are useless. They can be useful intermediate work. And a language model can suggest an approach that we might never have considered. The question is: how do we check it? If the model proposes a plan, does that plan actually achieve the goal, given the constraints? Asking it to tell us again that the plan is good isn’t an independent check.

So I would put the emphasis less on the slogan that these systems are thoughtless and more on the architecture around them. You can have a very powerful generator of candidate solutions, coupled with something that can verify those solutions and provide feedback. Then you can exploit what the language model does well without assuming that fluency gives you correctness.

And there’s a distinction here between saying a system cannot possibly reason and saying that a particular demonstration doesn’t establish reasoning. The latter is the more useful scientific claim. We should be asking what the evidence supports, what the failure modes are, and what would make the resulting system reliable.

r001.rationale: The response shifts emphasis from the slogan that systems are thoughtless to generator-and-verifier architecture, but it does not describe a shift from demonstrating inability to follow procedures toward framing chain of thought as prompt augmentation.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prompt augmentation or say that human involvement becomes less important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction I want to make more clearly is between generating a plausible reasoning trace and actually having a process that gives you some assurance that the reasoning is correct. Those are different things, and fluent language makes it very easy to conflate them.

With “Chain of Thoughtlessness,” the point isn’t that a language model can never produce a correct plan or a correct answer. It clearly can. The question is what you can conclude from that success. If it produces a sequence of steps that sounds reasonable, does that mean those steps respect the constraints of the problem? You have to check that independently. And asking the same model, “Are you sure?” doesn’t automatically give you an independent check.

So I would put the constructive part more prominently: these models can be very useful for proposing candidates. You can then combine them with a verifier that can reject an invalid candidate and provide feedback. The resulting system may solve problems very effectively. But we should understand where that reliability comes from, rather than attribute it all to the apparent reasoning in the generated text.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes plausible reasoning traces from verified reasoning and describes models proposing candidates for a verifier. It does not describe a shift from demonstrating that models cannot follow procedures to framing chain of thought as prompt augmentation.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss prompt augmentation or say that human involvement becomes less important.
